newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Woman to challenge warlords for Liberia presidency.
newsitem.headline: Woman to challenge warlords for Liberia presidency.

text.p: U.N. Development Programme Africa director Ellen Johnson-Sirleaf has entered the race for Liberia's May 30 presidential election, offering a feminine alternative to the men behind seven years of civil war.
Sirleaf told Reuters after winning the nomination of the newly formed Unity Party on Saturday that she had resigned her post with the United Nations.
Her opponents will include Charles Taylor, the man who launched the war in December 1989, and rival faction leader Alhaji Kromah.

"We believe that Liberia needs the Unity Party, the party that will unite Liberians and rebuild Liberia," she told a convention of several hundred supporters in Monrovia City Hall. "It's a party that will bring everyone together."

Election officials say that nine parties have registered to present candidates for the elections, part of a peace plan brokered by Liberia's West African neighbours and backed by their Nigerian-led West African peacekeeping force ECOMOG.
ECOMOG says it has gone a long way towards disarming the country's faction fighters.

"I have come to say yes to your call that I lead our country and save it from falling in the hands of the wrong people," Sirleaf told several thousand supporters after arriving at Monrovia's Spriggs Payne airfield on Friday.

Taylor and Kromah, sometime foes whose forces fought together against ethnic Krahn rivals during a flare-up in the war in Monrovia in April and May 1996, are both standing for the shattered country's top job.
Taylor, who repeatedly tried and failed to take the capital by force of arms, will run under the banner of his National Patriotic Party which opened its convention on Saturday.

Kromah, a Mandingo whose stronghold is in the west of Liberia, will represent his All Liberia Coalition Party which celebrated its registration on Saturday with drumming and dancing at party headquarters.
The other main warlords, Roosevelt Johnson and George Boley, will not be running for president.
Both come from the Krahn ethnic group which seized power in 1980, breaking the stranglehold of the descendants of the freed American slaves who founded the nation in 1847.

The civil war, which has killed well over 150,000 people, began as an attempt by Taylor and his allies to oust Master Sergeant Samuel Doe, who had staged a coup. But it disintegrated into a struggle for power among rival factions.

Boley, leader of the National Democratic Party of Liberia, Doe's party until he was killed in the war, joined an alliance of seven parties but lost the presidential slot to geophysicist Cletus Wotorson of the Liberia Action Party.
Johnson said he was going into business.
The election commission has yet to announce a formal election timetable. Electoral lists still have to be drawn up.

As many as half of Liberia's pre-war population of 2.5 million people have been displaced or have fled abroad. Several hundred thousand refugees are in neighbouring Ivory Coast, Guinea and Sierra Leone.
